title: Finite analytic ramification invariants and residue lifts
statement: All fields below are complete fields [def-weil-field] with compatible nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute values. For such a field $A$, write $A^\circ=\{x:|x|\le1\}$ for its valuation ring [def-trf-valuation-ring], $\widetilde A=A^\circ/\{x:|x|<1\}$ and $\Gamma_A=|A^\times|$. For a finite extension $B/A$ set $e(B/A)=[\Gamma_B:\Gamma_A]$, $f(B/A)=[\widetilde B:\widetilde A]$ and $d(B/A)=[B:A]/(e(B/A)f(B/A))$. Call it immediate if its value group and residue field equal those of $A$, unramified if $e=d=1$ and the residue extension is separable, and tame if $d=1$, its residue extension is separable and its ramification index is prime to the residue characteristic (with no index restriction in residue characteristic zero). A field extension is separable if every algebraic element has a minimal polynomial with distinct roots. Finite extensions of a complete field are complete for their extending absolute value, which is unique; their $e,f$ are finite positive integers. The three invariants $e,f,d$ are multiplicative in finite towers, and $d$ is a power of the positive residue characteristic; in residue characteristic zero $d=1$. Tame finite extensions are closed under composition, intermediate fields and base change to finite complete extensions (taking a field compositum). If $B/A$ is finite and $\widetilde B/\widetilde A$ is separable, there is an unramified intermediate field $A\subseteq U\subseteq B$ with $\widetilde U=\widetilde B$; unramified means the numerical and separability condition specified above. If $B/A$ is finite immediate and $A^\prime/A$ is finite tame, then $BA^\prime/A^\prime$ is immediate and $[BA^\prime:A^\prime]=[B:A]$. Finally for a complete ground field $k$, passing from a complete extension $A/k$ to a finite extension $B/A$ (complete for the extending absolute value) preserves the transcendence degree of $\widetilde A/\widetilde k$ and the rational rank of $\Gamma_A/\Gamma_k$ (the transcendence degree of $\widetilde B/\widetilde k$ and the rational rank of $\Gamma_B/\Gamma_k$ equal them); if the former is zero and $\widetilde k$ is algebraically closed then $\widetilde B=\widetilde A=\widetilde k$, and a finite-index extension of the divisible group $\Gamma_k$ inside $\mathbf R_{>0}$ is still $\Gamma_k$.

source.place: §2.1, printed pp. 8–9, ramification discussion and Lemma 2.1.5; §6.2 opening, p. 41 (invariants unchanged by finite extension); immediate/tame base-change consequence of the same ramification calculus.

proof.text: For every finite extension of $A$, the spectral-norm construction supplies an extending nonarchimedean absolute value. Uniqueness of the extending absolute value identifies it with the given one. Regarding the extension as a finite-dimensional normed $A$-space proves completeness. The complete field's valuation ring is henselian: apply the henselianity assertion of the completion-factors node to this field itself, whose completion is itself. Thus every ground field and every intermediate field to which Hensel lifting is applied below is complete and henselian.

source.place: section 2.1, analytic fields are henselian; Proposition 2.2.1, completed-field preliminaries

proof.text: The fundamental inequality gives positive finite integers $e,f$ and $ef\le[B:A]$, hence $d\ge1$. In $A\subset B\subset C$, enumerate cosets of $\Gamma_A$ in $\Gamma_B$ and of $\Gamma_B$ in $\Gamma_C$; their products enumerate cosets of $\Gamma_A$ in $\Gamma_C$ exactly once. Products of bases for the two residue-field extensions form a basis for the composite extension, and products of bases for the two field extensions do likewise. Thus $e,f,[C:A]$ multiply, and division of these equalities proves multiplicativity of $d$.

source.place: section 2.1, fundamental inequality preceding Lemma 2.1.2 and defect notation preceding Lemma 2.1.5

proof.text: First take a finite Galois extension $N/A$. The wild-kernel lemma supplies $T=N^P$ with $d(T/A)=1$, and $[N:T]=|P|$, $e(N/T)$ and $f(N/T)$ powers of $p$ when the residue characteristic is $p>0$. Thus $d(N/A)=d(N/T)$ is an integral power of $p$: its exponent is nonnegative by the fundamental inequality. In residue characteristic zero, $P=1$, so $T=N$ and the defect is one. For a finite separable $B/A$, put it inside such a Galois $N/A$. The same argument applies to $N/B$, which is also Galois by the intermediate-field Galois lemma. Dividing $d(N/A)$ by $d(N/B)$ and using $d(B/A)\ge1$ proves the assertion for $B/A$.

source.place: section 2.1, Lemma 2.1.5(iv), expanding the Galois wild-kernel input

proof.text: For arbitrary finite $B/A$, take its maximal separable subfield $S$. The separable-first theorem gives $B/S$ purely inseparable. In positive field characteristic the cited root tower gives $[B:S]=p^r$ and a common exponent $p^h$ with $x^{p^h}\in S$ for every $x\in B$. Consequently the finite group $\Gamma_B/\Gamma_S$ is a $p$-group and $\widetilde B/\widetilde S$ is finite purely inseparable, so both $e$ and $f$ are powers of $p$. Their product is at most $p^r$, proving that $d(B/S)$ is a nonnegative power of $p$. Multiply by the already proved $d(S/A)$. In field characteristic zero $S=B$; when the field characteristic is positive it equals the residue characteristic, so this covers all cases.

source.place: section 2.1, Lemma 2.1.5(iv), inseparable case; Stacks fields.tex, separable/purely-inseparable factorization

proof.text: Suppose $\widetilde B/\widetilde A$ is separable. Choose a primitive element $\bar b$ with monic minimal polynomial $\bar g$ of degree $f$. Lift its coefficients to $A^\circ$, obtaining monic $g$. In the henselian ring $B^\circ$, the simple residue root $\bar b$ lifts to $b$ satisfying $g(b)=0$. Put $U=A(b)$. Its residue field contains $\widetilde A(\bar b)=\widetilde B$, and is contained in $\widetilde B$, so they agree. On the other hand $[U:A]\le\deg g=f$. The fundamental inequality applied to $U/A$ forces $[U:A]=f$ and $e(U/A)=1$. Thus $d(U/A)=1$ and the residue extension is separable, as required. This includes $f=1$, where one may simply take $U=A$.

source.place: section 2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.5, first paragraph; direct simple-root realization of the residue lift

proof.text: In a tower of finite extensions, defects are positive integers by steps 3--4. If the composite has defect one, multiplicativity forces both defects to be one. Its ramification indices divide the composite index; a separable residue extension has separable intermediate and upper extensions. Hence intermediate fields of a tame extension, and the corresponding upper extensions, are tame. Conversely, if both successive extensions are tame, multiply $e,f,d$ and use transitivity of separability for $\widetilde A\subseteq\widetilde B\subseteq\widetilde C$ from the separable-permanence lemma to see that the composite is tame. The prime-to-$p$ condition is preserved under products and divisors. These arguments also work for $p=0$, with that condition omitted.

source.place: section 2.1, Lemma 2.1.5(iii), tower consequences of the numerical criterion

proof.text: Let $B/A$ be tame and $C/A$ finite. The root-envelope lemma puts $B$ inside $R=U(\alpha_i)$, with $U^\circ/A^\circ$ finite etale, $\alpha_i^{n_i}=a_i\in U^\times$, and $n_i$ prime to the residue characteristic. Base change the finite etale algebra to $C^\circ$. The homomorphism to $(UC)^\circ$ selects its local factor by the inverse image of the maximal ideal. The henselian valuation etale-factor lemma identifies that factor's fraction field with $UC$ and gives its valuation ring finite etale over $C^\circ$. The same equations $\alpha_i^{n_i}=a_i$ now have coefficients in $UC$, and its field still contains all the required roots of unity. The converse direction of the root-envelope lemma, over $C$, shows $RC/C$ is tame. Its intermediate field $BC/C$ is tame by step 6. Completeness of all fields used here is step 1; finiteness of the tensor algebra and its local factor is preserved by finite base change.

source.place: section 2.1, maximal tame extension; Gabber--Ramero 6.2.14--6.2.18, finite root description and base change

proof.text: For the immediate base change, put $L=A'$ and choose $t_i\in L^\times$ representing $\Gamma_L/\Gamma_A$ and units $u_j\in L^\circ$ lifting a $\widetilde A$-basis of $\widetilde L$, including $1$. The $t_i u_j$ form an orthogonal $A$-basis: different $i$ have distinct value cosets; for fixed $i$, divide the coefficients by one of maximal absolute value and use residue independence to prevent cancellation. Their number is $ef=[L:A]$. If $B/A$ is immediate, the identical argument over $B$ works because $\Gamma_B=\Gamma_A$ and $\widetilde B=\widetilde A$. Thus they remain independent over $B$. Their $B$-span is the image of $B\otimes_A L$, a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field and therefore $BL$; this proves $[BL:B]=[L:A]$ and by tower degrees $[BL:L]=[B:A]$. For each nonzero coefficient $b\in B$, immediacy gives $a\in A$ with $|b-a|<|b|$: match its value by an element of $A$ and then match its unit residue. Approximate all the finitely many coefficients in any $x\in BL$ this way. Orthogonality gives $y\in L$ with $|x-y|<|x|$. Hence $|x|=|y|$, and if $|x|=1$ then $x$ and $y$ have the same residue. It follows that $BL/L$ is immediate. The argument uses only defectlessness of $L/A$, already part of tameness.

source.place: section 2.1, orthogonal-basis characterization of Cartesian extensions immediately before Lemma 2.1.5; explicit immediate-base-change calculation

proof.text: For $k\subset A\subset B$, the residue extension $\widetilde B/\widetilde A$ is finite and algebraic by the degree bound, so a transcendence basis for $\widetilde A/\widetilde k$ is still one for $\widetilde B/\widetilde k$: independence is unchanged and algebraicity is transitive. The quotient $\Gamma_B/\Gamma_A$ is finite; tensoring the inclusions modulo $\Gamma_k$ with $\mathbf Q$ therefore gives an isomorphism. Explicitly, every class upstairs has a positive multiple downstairs, so its rational span is the same, and clearing denominators checks injectivity. This proves the two invariance assertions, in arbitrary cardinal dimension. If the residue transcendence degree is zero and $\widetilde k$ algebraically closed, both residue fields are algebraic over $\widetilde k$, hence equal it. Finally if a subgroup $D\subset\mathbf R_{>0}$ is divisible and $D\subset H$ has finite index, each $h\in H$ has $h^n\in D$ for some $n>0$. Choose $d\in D$ with $d^n=h^n$; injectivity of the positive real $n$-th power map gives $h=d$. Thus $H=D$.

source.place: section 6.2, opening paragraph, invariance of E and F under finite extension; Remark 6.2.2 for divisible value groups
